clue.text: We pen and pen with arms outstretched

definitions.text: We pen and pen with arms outstretched

indicators.note: the letters are stretched out of shape and laid out afresh, as limbs are flung wide

explanation.surface: Writers describe themselves busily scribbling away, arms flung wide as they work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' and 'with' are links; the whole clue also describes journalists, who pen copy for a living, so it doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalists are the people who write the copy, so the clue's picture of busy scribblers describes them.

clue.text: School run — true/false?

indicators.note: something false is not true to form, so these letters are wrongly arranged

explanation.surface: A quiz question asks whether a statement about the school run is true or false.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false' looks like half of a quiz option but it signals rearranging RUN and TRUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To school a child is to train and bring them up, which is a synonym for raising them with care.

clue.text: Open up relish, which is unfriendly

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: an open wound is raw
to relish something is to like it

explanation.surface: Someone opens a jar of relish, apparently a hostile act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open up' looks like one phrase meaning unseal; here 'Open' gives RAW and 'up' turns it.
explanation.definitionFit: Warlike behaviour is hostile and aggressive, a synonym for unfriendly.

clue.text: Mollycoddling sick man with grippe

indicators.note: sick suggests the letters are disordered, as an unwell body is

explanation.surface: Someone fusses over a man laid low with flu.
explanation.walkthrough: Grippe is an old word for influenza; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mollycoddling and pampering are synonyms: both mean overindulging someone.

clue.text: Birds dropping in for smokes

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away, so these letters leave the word

parts.note: puffins are seabirds

explanation.surface: Birds drop in to visit while someone has a cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping in' reads as visiting; here 'dropping' removes the letters of 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A puff is a draw on a cigarette, so puffs are smokes in the casual sense.

clue.text: Practical person read half a directory

indicators.note: half means only the first two of the four letters of read are kept

parts.note: a directory is a list of names

explanation.surface: A down-to-earth person reads only half a phone directory.
explanation.definitionFit: A realist deals with things as they are, which makes them a practical, unsentimental person.

clue.text: Nearly kill intimate circle

indicators.note: nearly means stopping just short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to kill is to end a life
intimate friends are close

explanation.surface: An assassin almost finishes off someone's inner circle of friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' trims END to EN. 'circle' is a verb here, not the noun it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: To circle something is to go round it and so surround or enclose it.

clue.text: Carousel found in tight hole in clay

parts.note: tight is slang for drunk, as is merry
clay is a kind of ground, and a hole (the round letter O) goes inside it, just after its G

explanation.surface: A fairground ride is discovered stuck in a hole in clay soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' is a link. Tight is slang for drunk, as is merry.
explanation.definitionFit: A carousel is a fairground roundabout, the ride also called a merry-go-round.

clue.text: Beard rumpled a bit? Must be stretched skin

indicators.note: a bit means only a piece of the two words, the run across their join, is taken

explanation.surface: A man's beard looks slightly messed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rumpled' looks like an anagram signal but the letters are taken in order; 'Must be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The tympanic membrane is a taut membrane in the ear, a stretched skin like a drum head.

clue.text: Working-class symbol is even better

parts.note: an even surface is flat
to cap something is to better or outdo it

explanation.surface: A comment on social status says something is even better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' is a verb here, as in capping a story; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth cap worn by northern working men became an emblem of the working class in Britain.

clue.text: Frank's in poor health, but making smooth progress

parts.note: plain means frank, and the 's gives S
ailing means unwell

explanation.surface: Frank is unwell but recovering steadily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank's' looks like a man's name; it is the adjective frank plus 's. 'but making' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain sailing is an idiom for easy, untroubled progress.

clue.text: Marry again with a group engaged in endless dance

indicators.note: engaged in means caught up inside, so the group sits within the dance
endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance
a unit is a group of people

explanation.surface: A couple wed for a second time while a band plays during an unending dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a' is a link; the dance is the Scottish reel, which loses its last letter before the group goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To reunite is to bring together again, which here stands for remarrying.

clue.text: Philosopher with positive slant, one about Australia

indicators.note: about signals the one coming beside Australia, attached in the answer after it

parts.note: spin is the positive slant a press officer puts on news
Oz is a nickname for Australia
a means one

explanation.surface: A thinker with an optimistic outlook writes about Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Spinoza was a 17th-century Dutch philosopher; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Baruch Spinoza was a Dutch rationalist philosopher, so the name is an example of the category.

clue.text: The exaggerator's swans

parts.note: the saying that all someone's birds are swans mocks a person who overrates ordinary things; the reality is plainer birds

explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'all his geese are swans' describes someone who exaggerates, so the exaggerator's swans are really plain birds.

clue.text: Agent to remain affected in the pub

indicators.note: in places the remaining and affected pieces inside the pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub
to be is to exist or remain
twee means affectedly quaint

explanation.surface: A secret agent is told to stay put in the pub, acting oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: TWEE is British for sugary and over-dainty.
explanation.definitionFit: An in-between is a go-between or intermediary, someone acting as an agent between parties.

clue.text: Poor opportunities for snooker players?

definitions.meaning: unlucky turns of fortune that offer little
a snooker break is a run of scoring shots, and a poor one is a weak run

explanation.definitionFit: Unlucky breaks are bad luck in general, and in snooker a break is a turn of scoring shots.

clue.text: Pepped up and angry about an accusation

indicators.note: about means one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: red stands for angry, as in seeing red
a charge is a formal accusation

explanation.surface: Someone is energised and furious over an accusation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an' is a link; seeing red is the idiom behind angry here, and the accusation is surrounded.
explanation.definitionFit: Recharged means given fresh energy, a synonym for pepped up.

clue.text: It moves very quickly if spotted

definitions.text: It moves very quickly if spotted

parts.words: It moves very quickly if spotted
parts.note: reads as something that bolts when noticed, but describes the fastest land animal, whose coat is spotted

explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is the fastest land animal and has a spotted coat.

clue.text: Fresh raw rice for high fliers

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Uncooked rice is served to people with high ambitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Aircrew fly aircraft, so they are high fliers in the literal sense.

clue.text: Doctor wants child to have a coffee

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor wants a child to drink a coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wants' and 'to have' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocha is a fine-quality coffee named after the Yemeni port.

clue.text: Wine and a half ripe cheese to be sent up

indicators.note: in a down entry, sent up means the pieces are read from the bottom upwards
half means the first two of the four letters of ripe are kept

parts.note: Edam is a Dutch cheese

explanation.surface: Wine and a half-ripe cheese are sent up to someone's room.
explanation.walkthrough: A, RI and EDAM are written in that order and then the whole run is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Madeira is a fortified wine from the Portuguese island of that name.

clue.text: What Mrs Mopp did, having good education

parts.note: clean living is good, morally sound living

explanation.surface: A charwoman tidied up and had a decent schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Mopp was the cleaning lady in the wartime BBC radio comedy ITMA; 'having' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Mopp was a charwoman, so what she did was dust and scrub.

clue.text: Turn up her aunt when moving

indicators.note: moving suggests the letters shift into a new order

explanation.surface: An aunt turns up when the family is moving house.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn up something hidden is to dig it out or discover it.

clue.text: He needs a length cut in half for a bright girl

indicators.note: cut in half means only the first three of the six letters of length are kept

explanation.surface: A man needs a length of material cut in half for a clever girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs a' and 'for' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek name Helen is linked to words for torch or light, so it suits a bright girl.

clue.text: Oxygen carrier left next to prison

parts.note: red is the colour of the political left
a cell is a prison room

explanation.surface: A left-wing prisoner is put in the cell next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'next to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Red blood corpuscles carry oxygen round the body via haemoglobin.

clue.text: Plover made right with Dettol

indicators.note: made means fashioned, so the letters are put together in a new form

explanation.surface: A wading bird is cleaned up properly with antiseptic.
explanation.walkthrough: Dettol is a British brand of antiseptic liquid; the dotterel (also spelt this way) is a plover.
explanation.definitionFit: The dotterel is a small migratory wader of the plover family.

clue.text: Soon about half strength on the Rhone

indicators.note: about means soon wraps around the half strength

parts.note: anon is an old word for soon

indicators.note: half means only the first three of the six letters are kept

parts.note: vigour means strength

explanation.surface: Someone will soon be at half strength somewhere on the Rhone.
explanation.walkthrough: Strength is spelt the British way, with OU, so halving it leaves three letters; anon is an old word for soon.
explanation.definitionFit: Avignon, the old papal city in Provence, stands on the River Rhone.

clue.text: Expose tactics by removing glove

definitions.meaning: to reveal one's plans, like a card player laying cards face up
literally baring the palm by taking off a glove

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means revealing your intentions, as a card player shows the cards held.
